First off, i'm from the USA and previously identified with the Democratic Party. After some 'soul searching' I guess you could say, and actually analyzing what I believe in i've started to look into other forms of political thought. My main question is the title, but also I would like to see some other point of views that I may have missed.
What does Libertarianism mean to you?

Well, technically, what Libertarianism means to me is strong support of the U.S. Libertarian party.

What libertarianism (lowercase "l") means to me, on the other hand, is an ideological responsibility to protect and preserve all forms of freedom from any and all institutions, entities, or individuals that might seek to oppress those natural freedoms without the subject's consent.

Sorry for being pedantic.

Libertarianism is a form of "egoist" philosophy. The core of this philosophical principle is that nobody can know you better than yourself, so you are the one who is best qualified to make decisions related to your well-being. Conversely this means that you are not qualified to make decisions for others.

This means that, as a libertarian, I am averse to the state making decisions on issues like who someone can or can't marry, what foods they can or can't eat, etc. Generally situations where the state makes a choice for you is a situation where I see freedom being inhibited while the power of the state grows, and this is something I dislike because I believe that I am better able to make decisions for myself than the government.

This also extends to economic issues though. Myself, and many other libertarians included, believe in the concept that economic freedom and social freedom are intertwined. A society that lacks economic freedom can never truly have social freedom because your livelihood and well-being is dependent on a system that you may be at odds with, and being in conflict with an idea of the system would risk you losing all that you have.

It seems vague, but it's a complicated issue. For more information I'd recommend reading about The Road to Serfdom, a book written by an Austrian economist during the Nazi party's rise to power. He explains how little-by-little people were forced to give up economic freedoms for the good of their social ideology, but then even that became quickly perverted and twisted, as all power was given to the state and the state made all decisions on what you could or couldn't do, say or couldn't say, etc., etc.

In an economic sense though, libertarians (and myself included) generally believe that the government is not better at making decisions for a business than the business is for itself, and that government intervention stifles growth and weakens the economy. A good example I like to use is the Affordable Care Act, which has a stipulation in it that no health insurance company is permitted to spend more than 20% of its revenue on administrative costs (so 80% to covering medical expenses). Sounds good, right? More money going to paying for healthcare, less to line the pockets of "greedy" executives? Well no, it's actually a horrible plan. Insurance companies that spent more than 20% of revenue on administrative costs were actually ones that were usually better at negotiating contracts and able to pay less for the same amount of healthcare. The new system actually gives insurance companies a strong incentive to keep the cost of healthcare going up, as now the company can grow if the product (that all people are mandated to purchase now) becomes more expensive.

All in all we strive for minimal government and maximum freedom. We embrace ideas such as education vouchers (proposed by Friedman, and used to wild success in Finland, a country with perhaps the best primary education system in the world), flat taxes, private licensing, etc.

The Non-Aggression Principle (also called the Non-Aggression Axiom) is the idea that each person has the right to make his or her own choices in life so long as they do not involve aggression, defined as the initiation of force against others. It is considered by many to be the defining principle of libertarianism. More technically, the principle asserts that aggression, a term defined by proponents as any encroachment on another person's life, liberty, or justly acquired property, or an attempt to obtain from another via deceit what could not be consensually obtained, is always illegitimate. According to some libertarians the NAP and property rights are closely linked, since what aggression is depends on what a person's rights are.[1] Aggression, for the purposes of NAP, is defined as initiating or threatening violence against a person or legitimately owned property of another.

-- wikipedia
